bracket: [Textbook answer-key error, self-refuting on the chapter's own rule. The key prints the two isoelectronic sets as \(\text{Na}^{+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Ar}, \text{S}^{2-}, \text{K}^{+}\), placing \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) with the ten-electron species. Counting by the chapter's own rule (electrons \(= Z -\) charge), calcium has \(Z = 20\) so \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) has \(20 - 2 = 18\) electrons and belongs with \(\text{Ar}\) (18), \(\text{S}^{2-}\) (16 + 2 = 18) and \(\text{K}^{+}\) (19 - 1 = 18), while only \(\text{Na}^{+}\) (10) and \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) (10) form the ten-electron set. The answer below gives the corrected grouping with the electron count shown for every species so the reader can check it directly.]

[Textbook errors — TWO, and the second means the question has no single right answer. (1) UNIT: the table heads the velocities \(\text{cm s}^{-1}\); they must be read as \(\text{m s}^{-1}\), or Planck's constant comes out near \(10^{-38}\), four orders of magnitude from its accepted value. (2) THE DATA ARE NOT SELF-CONSISTENT. Einstein's photoelectric equation makes kinetic energy linear in \(1/\lambda\), so the three \((\lambda, v)\) points should be collinear and they are not — the answer therefore depends entirely on which PAIR of rows you use: 500 and 450 nm give \(h = 8.49 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 = 531\,\text{nm}\); 500 and 400 nm give \(h = 6.72 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 = 540\,\text{nm}\); 450 and 400 nm give \(h = 5.30 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 = 595\,\text{nm}\). The printed key's \(530.9\,\text{nm}\) reproduces the 500/450 pairing exactly — but that pairing implies a Planck's constant 28% above the accepted \(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\), which is precisely the quantity part (b) asks the student to determine, and the key prints no value of \(h\) at all, so its own inconsistency never surfaces. The answer below uses the 500/400 pairing, which returns \(h = 6.72 \times 10^{-34}\), within 1.4% of the accepted value; a least-squares fit to all three points gives \(h = 6.66 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 \approx 546\,\text{nm}\). Expect \(531\,\text{nm}\) in any answer key.]

[Textbook answer-key error, self-refuting against the key's own second figure. The key prints the energy required as \(2.08 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{ergs}\); the question's own datum gives \(2.18 \times 10^{-11} \times (1 - 1/25) = 2.0928 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{ergs}\), which neither rounds nor truncates to 2.08. The key refutes itself in the same entry: it goes on to print a wavelength of \(950\,\text{Å}\), and \(2.0928 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{ergs}\) corresponds to \(949.8\,\text{Å}\) while its own \(2.08 \times 10^{-11}\) would give \(956\,\text{Å}\). So the wavelength it prints is the one our energy produces, not the one its own energy produces.]

[Textbook answer-key error of sign, and THE QUESTION'S OWN STEM REFUTES IT. The key prints the fifth-orbit energy as a POSITIVE quantity — but the stem itself supplies the first-orbit energy as \(-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\), negative, and \(E_n = E_1/n^2\) divides that by \(25\), an operation that cannot change its sign. So the key contradicts the datum printed in the question it answers. The physics agrees: an electron bound in an atom has negative total energy by construction, the zero of the scale being the free electron at rest, which is exactly why ionisation requires energy to be supplied. Only the sign is at issue; the magnitude the key prints, \(8.72 \times 10^{-20}\), is correct.]

[Textbook answer-key error in the DIRECTION of the ordering. The question asks for the species arranged in order of INCREASING size, and the key prints its list in DECREASING order. The sequence of species the key names is right; it is the stated direction that is reversed, so a reader comparing answers should compare the two lists end-to-end rather than term-by-term.]
